newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi Arabia welcomes BIS membership offer.
newsitem.headline: Saudi Arabia welcomes BIS membership offer.

text.p: Saudi Arabia on Tuesday welcomed an offer to join the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), a move which bankers said would boost the oil giant's standing in international financial circles.

The official Saudi Press Agency said the Saudi Arabian Monetary Authority's (SAMA) joining BIS underscored "the importance of the Saudi economy and the position of the Saudi Arabian kingdom and its reputation in financial circles."

The Basle, Switzerland-based BIS, central bank to the world's central banks, said on Monday it would invite nine major new central banks across the world to join its ranks. This is the first time in 25 years the BIS has enlarged its membership.
Bankers and economists in Saudi Arabia welcomed the news.
"It is a good development. It is a vote of confidence," said Henry Azzam, chief economist at the Jeddah-based National Commercial Bank.
"It is a positive move because it will bring Saudi Arabia more into the world economy," said a Western diplomat in Riyadh.
"The Saudi banking system is a very strong one and this (BIS membership) is a reflection of the importance given to the Saudi economy by the rest of thw world," he added.

To become members in the exclusive club of the world's most powerful central banks, SAMA must purchase an undisclosed number of BIS shares that are not held by the other members. Currently there are 32 members, only five of which are not European.

Asked what else was likely to be required of SAMA, Azzam said: "It is unlikely to change much here, other than possibly (to get SAMA) to provide more information on monetary changes regularly to the BIS."

Analysts said the benefits of joining the world's oldest international financial institution were mainly the improved contact -- through regular meetings -- with the world's most influential central bankers, including those of the Group of 10.
"It means they will be in touch regularly with governors of major central banks," one said.
"They will know more about what is happening and have a clearer idea on what is affecting the exchange rate of the dollar and dollar interest rates," he added.
Analysts said most banks in the oil-rich kingdom were already adhering to guidelines set up by the BIS, in particular the suggested capital adequacy ratio of eight percent.
